course.title: DNS Fundamentals
course.description: Learn how domain names lead to DNS answers. Follow a lookup, build common records, predict cached results and recognise lookup failures through hands-on practice. Six beginner lessons, about 55 minutes, and no videos. All lessons are free previews; saving completion requires an account with course access.

lessons.title: Find the name inside a URL
lessons.description: Separate a hostname from the scheme, port, path and query in a web URL.
lessons.content:
Before you start

By the end of this lesson, you can find a hostname inside a web URL. You only need a browser; no terminal or domain account is required. All names and addresses in this course are fictional examples.

Explain

DNS stands for Domain Name System. It stores information under names. An address lookup is one use; DNS also holds other kinds of records.

A web URL contains more than a name. In https://learn.example.com/start?mode=practice, the hostname is learn.example.com. The scheme, path and query are not part of it.

Dots separate DNS labels. Read learn.example.com. from right to left to follow the hierarchy: root, com, example, learn. The final dot represents the root; web URLs usually omit it.

Worked example

For https://shop.example.com:8443/cart, write shop.example.com as the hostname. Leave out https://, the port 8443 and /cart.

Practice

Write only the hostname from each URL:
1. https://docs.example.com/intro
2. https://mail.example.org:8443/inbox?view=new
3. https://example.net/

Describe where docs sits in docs.example.com.

Hint: Find the name after //. Stop before a port, slash or query. Write your answers on paper or in your own notes. Then select Reveal self-check answers to compare them. These written answers are not collected or stored.

Recap

You can identify a hostname without confusing it with the full URL. Next, follow who answers a lookup.

Self-check — read after practising

1. docs.example.com
2. mail.example.org
3. example.net
The docs label is beneath example.com; example is beneath com, which is beneath the root. If you included a path or port, remove it. Do not invent www or drop the first label.

lessons.title: Follow a DNS lookup
lessons.description: Predict the next message, then compare a cold lookup with a valid cached answer.
lessons.content:
Explain

Your device asks a recursive resolver to find an answer. An authoritative server answers from the zone data it serves. A zone is an administered portion of DNS.

A means an IPv4 address record. TLD means top-level domain; com is one example.

When the resolver has no useful cached data, it follows referrals. The root directs it toward com; com directs it toward the servers for example.com. A referral tells it where to ask next, not the requested address.

Worked example

For our fictional app.example.com A lookup, the device asks the resolver. The resolver asks a root server, then a com server, then the authoritative server for example.com. It receives 192.0.2.10 and returns it to the device. The resolver, not your browser, follows these referrals in this model.

Practice

Each stage in the walkthrough combines a query and its reply; it is not a single packet.

1. Choose who receives the query.
2. Choose the result of that stage: request, referral or answer.
3. Select Check step and read the explanation.
4. Select Next step to continue. You can change a choice and check again.

After the cold lookup, choose warm cache. Explain which outside queries are skipped and why.

Hint: Check whether the resolver already holds the requested answer.

Recap

You can separate the resolver from the servers it asks. A valid cached answer can shorten the path. The model omits forwarding, name-server address discovery, query-name minimisation and errors. It is not a packet capture, and all answers are fictional.

coldSteps.explanation: Your device asks the resolver to find the A answer.
The resolver asks the root server. The root replies with a referral toward com, not the final address.
The resolver asks a com server. It replies with a referral toward the servers for example.com.
The resolver asks the authoritative server. Its reply supplies the requested A answer.
The resolver returns the answer and keeps a cached copy.

warmSteps.explanation: The device asks the recursive resolver again.
The valid A answer is already cached. No root, TLD or authoritative query is needed in this model.

lessons.title: Choose the right record
lessons.description: Build six fictional DNS records for address, alias, mail, text and name-server jobs.
lessons.content:
Explain

A record has an owner name, a type and a value. The owner is the name you are adding information to. The value is the address, target name or text you want to store.

Choose the type for the job:
A: an IPv4 address.
AAAA: an IPv6 address.
CNAME: an alias pointing to another DNS name, not a web URL.
MX: a mail server name with a preference number; lower numbers are preferred.
TXT: text; an application may use it for verification.
NS: a name server for a zone.

Worked example

Give app.example.com the A value 192.0.2.10. To make www.example.com an alias, use CNAME with value app.example.com. Do not enter https://app.example.com/start: an alias does not specify a page path.

Practice

1. Read the job on each card.
2. Enter the owner name: the name receiving the record.
3. Choose a record type and copy the supplied value.
4. For MX, also enter the mail preference.
5. Select Check records after completing all six cards.

Read the feedback beside each card. Edit a mistaken field, then check again. Reset records clears all six cards.

Hint: Decide whether the value is an address, a name or text. Mail selection also needs a preference.

Recap

You can choose a record for each job. A and AAAA can coexist at app.example.com. In this exercise, a CNAME owner has no other records. These cards are not a complete zone file or delegation setup, and no real DNS is changed.

tasks.hint: Use the record type for an IPv4 address.
tasks.explanation: A stores the supplied IPv4 address.

tasks.hint: IPv6 has its own address record type.
tasks.explanation: AAAA stores the supplied IPv6 address.

tasks.prompt: Make www.example.com an alias of app.example.com.
tasks.hint: An alias points to another DNS name, not an IP address or URL.
tasks.explanation: CNAME maps the alias name to app.example.com.

tasks.prompt: Select mail.example.com as the mail server for example.com with preference 10.
tasks.hint: Mail routing uses a server name and a preference number.
tasks.explanation: MX selects mail.example.com with preference 10, not its IP address.

tasks.prompt: Store the text course-verification=demo at example.com.
tasks.hint: Choose the record type that stores text.
tasks.explanation: TXT stores this case-sensitive verification text.

tasks.prompt: Identify ns1.example.net as a name server for the example.com zone.
tasks.hint: Name-server information is different from a host address.
tasks.explanation: NS identifies a name server serving the zone.

lessons.title: Predict what the cache returns
lessons.description: Use virtual time to predict an old cached answer, expiry and a refreshed TTL.
lessons.content:
Explain

A cache is a stored copy of an earlier answer. TTL means time to live, measured in seconds. It limits how long that copy may be kept; a real cache may discard it earlier.

The authoritative answer is the value supplied by the server serving the zone. Editing it does not replace an answer that another resolver has already cached.

Our fixed model uses one resolver and one A record. It keeps the cached entry until expiry, with no early eviction, prefetch, stale-answer serving or network delay.

Worked example

At time 0, the resolver caches 192.0.2.10 for 300 seconds. At time 60, its remaining TTL is 300 − 60 = 240 seconds. A query still uses the cached value.

Practice

The authority changes the answer to 192.0.2.20 at time 120. Query at 120, 299, 300 and 301 seconds using the timeline below. For each query, enter the IPv4 address and remaining TTL in whole seconds. Select Check prediction, read the explanation, then select Next query.

At the exact expiry time, process expiry before the query. A refreshed entry gets a new 300-second TTL; a cache hit does not restart it.

Hint: Track when the resolver stored the answer, not when the authority changed it. A successful refresh starts a new TTL.

Recap

You can distinguish authoritative and cached values. The model does not mean that every real resolver changes at the same instant. Reset to replay from time 0; do not carry future cache state backward.

lessons.title: Read the evidence before changing DNS
lessons.description: Distinguish missing names, missing record types, lookup failures and timeouts.
lessons.content:
Explain

NXDOMAIN: the queried name does not exist according to the server that replied.
NODATA: the name exists, but the requested record type is absent. This is not a separate response code; the response uses NOERROR.
SERVFAIL: the lookup failed; that alone does not identify one cause.
Timeout: no response arrived within the waiting period. This does not prove that the name is missing.

Worked example

In our fictional zone, ipv4-only.example.com has A but no AAAA record. An authoritative AAAA reply is NOERROR, contains no AAAA answer and includes the zone's SOA information. This is NODATA, not NXDOMAIN. SOA carries zone information; its fields are outside this lesson.

Practice

Classify each observation and suggest one safe next check:
1. A query for typo.example.com receives NXDOMAIN.
2. The worked AAAA query receives NODATA.
3. A resolver returns SERVFAIL with no extra details.
4. A request receives no reply before its timeout.

Write your answers in your own notes, then select Reveal self-check answers to compare them. These written answers are not collected. No commands or record changes are needed for this practice.

Hint: Was there a reply? Did it describe a missing name, missing type or failure?

Recap

Separate evidence from a guessed cause before suggesting a repair.

Self-check — read after practising

1. NXDOMAIN: recheck spelling and the intended name.
2. NODATA: confirm the requested type and whether IPv6 is intended.
3. SERVFAIL: gather more resolver or authoritative evidence before assigning a cause.
4. Timeout: check connectivity and whether the resolver is reachable.

These checks are not guaranteed fixes. An empty NOERROR answer containing a referral is not NODATA merely because it is empty.

lessons.title: Check your understanding
lessons.description: Apply what you learned in eight questions with explanations and unlimited retry.
lessons.content:
Choose one best answer for every question. Select Check answers to read the explanations, including those for correct choices. Review the matching lesson for anything you missed, then use Reset quiz to retry.

Hint: Separate the name from the URL, referrals from answers, and the authoritative value from the cached value.

Recap

Explain one lookup step, one record choice and one cache prediction in your own words. This self-check is practice, not a verified assessment. Answers and scores reset on reload. Marking the lesson complete is independent of your score.

questions.prompt: What is the hostname in https://support.example.org:8443/help?
questions.explanation: Leave scheme, port and path out of the hostname. Review Find the name inside a URL.

questions.prompt: Who follows referrals in our cold-lookup model?

choices.text: The mail server selected by MX

questions.explanation: The recursive resolver follows referrals in this model. Review Follow a DNS lookup.

questions.prompt: With a valid cached answer, what happens in our warm-lookup model?

choices.text: The resolver must query the root again
The resolver deletes the answer before using it
The resolver answers without root, TLD or authoritative queries
The browser edits the authoritative zone

questions.explanation: A valid cached answer removes the need for those outside queries here. Review Follow a DNS lookup.

questions.prompt: Which record type stores 2001:db8::10 as a host address?
questions.explanation: AAAA carries IPv6; A carries IPv4. Review Choose the right record.

questions.prompt: Which value belongs in a CNAME pointing to app.example.com?
questions.explanation: CNAME takes a target name, not a URL, address or MX-style preference. Review Choose the right record.

questions.prompt: In a fresh run with TTL 300, initial answer 192.0.2.10 and an authority change to 192.0.2.20 at t=120, what does a query at t=299 return?
questions.explanation: Original expiry is t=300; the old cached value has one second left. Review Predict what the cache returns.

questions.prompt: An authoritative reply confirms an existing name has no requested AAAA record. Its code is NOERROR. What is this result called?
questions.explanation: An absent type at an existing name is NODATA, not missing-name NXDOMAIN. Review Read the evidence before changing DNS.

questions.prompt: A resolver returns SERVFAIL without further details. What is justified?

choices.text: The website definitely needs a new A record
The lookup failed; gather more evidence about the cause
The name definitely does not exist

questions.explanation: SERVFAIL alone does not prove a specific cause. Review Read the evidence before changing DNS.
